That's worth pausing on, because it's genuinely non-obvious — and it explains every performance symptom you've seen. Here's what `reindex` actually does, plainly:

**It runs a neural network on your CPU, about a thousand times.** Step by step:

1. Your code gets chopped into ~1,000 chunks (functions, classes, doc sections), plus one chunk per ledger entry and session summary.
2. For **each chunk**, a 160MB transformer model — a small cousin of the models behind ChatGPT/Claude, specialized for code — runs a full inference pass on your CPU and produces a list of 768 numbers: a "meaning fingerprint" of that chunk.
3. Those fingerprints go into the local SQLite file. When you `ask` something, your question gets fingerprinted the same way, and the chunks whose numbers sit *closest* to your question's numbers are the relevant ones — that's how "why don't we use redis" finds the session-cookie change without sharing a single keyword.

So a reindex isn't file I/O or parsing — it's **~1,000 ML inference runs on your processor**. That's why it takes tens of minutes, why memory ballooned until the native runtime fell over, and why a GPU (built for exactly this math) or a cloud API (someone else's GPU) changes it from minutes to seconds.

Worth knowing alongside that:

- **Nothing leaves your machine today.** This was the deliberate "offline by default" privacy decision — and the CPU pain is precisely the price of it. The Bedrock option is the other side of that same coin: your chunk text would go to AWS, vectors come back, and it becomes fast and nearly free. It's a privacy-for-speed trade, which is why it sits behind an explicit consent flag rather than a default.
- **The index is disposable.** It's a derived cache — not part of your repo's data, never synced, deletable and rebuildable at any time. The ledger, sessions, and identity live in git and don't depend on it.
- **Most of the system doesn't need it.** `log --intent`, `show`, `report`, the review timeline, session traces, and the core of `blame --why` all read git directly. Only the *semantic* features — `ask` and the search-flavored parts — consume the index. Even then, the keyword half of retrieval works with no index vectors at all.

Knowing all that, the Bedrock question I left with you is really this, stated honestly: **are you comfortable with your code's text passing through AWS in exchange for indexing that's ~50× faster and costs about a cent per full run?** If yes, I'll build the Bedrock embedder. If you'd rather keep everything on-machine, the GPU path (DirectML) gets much of the same speedup with zero privacy trade, at the cost of more engineering. Both are now written up in the roadmap's Tier 0 — there's no wrong answer, just a real choice.

Now *that's* the right question for your situation — an NVIDIA card changes the picture completely, because it gets you the cloud-grade speedup with **zero privacy trade, zero AWS keys, zero per-token cost**. Let me ground it in your actual hardware first:

cd C:/src/git-for-ai/packages/core && pnpm build && pnpm vitest run src/query 2>&1 | grep -E "Tests |failed" && cd ../cli && pnpm build && pnpm vitest run 2>&1 | grep -E "Tests |failed"
cd C:/src/git-for-ai && grep -rn "\"@types/node\"" packages/*/package.json && ls node_modules/.pnpm | grep -i "@types+node" | head -5 && grep -n "import { spawn }" packages/cli/src/commands/review.ts

cd C:/src/git-for-ai && grep -rn "types/node" packages/cli/package.json packages/core/package.json packages/desktop/package.json package.json 2>/dev/null; ls node_modules/.pnpm 2>/dev/null | grep -i "types+node" | head; grep -n "spawn" packages/cli/src/commands/review.ts | head -3

cd C:/src/git-for-ai/packages/cli && pnpm add -D @types/node@^26.1.1 2>&1 | tail -2 && cd ../core && pnpm add -D @types/node@^26.1.1 2>&1 | tail -2 && cd ../cli && pnpm build && pnpm vitest run 2>&1 | grep -E "Tests |failed"

cd C:/src/git-for-ai && git add packages/core/src/query/types.ts packages/core/src/query/enrich.ts packages/core/src/query/engine.ts packages/core/src/query/synthesis.ts packages/core/src/query/engine.test.ts packages/cli/src/bin.ts architecture/CLI_REFERENCE.md packages/cli/package.json packages/core/package.json pnpm-lock.yaml && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
ask gains a recency floor; reindex can no longer die silently

Root-caused from a live owner question ("what was the most recent
change and why") that returned architecture docs instead of an answer.

Recency floor (core/query): askQuestion now always appends the N most
recent changes' effective ledger entries (default 5) as additional
cited sources, read directly from git - immune to index staleness,
which was half of the live failure. Embedding similarity has no
concept of time; no chunk text resembles "most recent", so temporal
questions previously retrieved noise. Sources already found
semantically are not duplicated (they gain the "recency" match side);
the synthesis prompt marks recency sources as chronology so the model
can reason over the created_at dates it already receives. kinds
filters that exclude ledger content skip the floor; recent: 0
disables. Applies automatically to CLI ask, /api/ask, and the MCP ask
tool (all route through askQuestion). Known scope edge: the
--since/--until composed path bypasses it (its temporal bounds are
explicit). Regression test recreates the exact live question against
a change the index has never seen.

Reindex silent-death guard (bin.ts): the other half of the live
failure - a native onnxruntime OOM stranded the inference promise,
the event loop drained, and Node exited 0 mid-run with no error. A
beforeExit sentinel now turns that into an explicit failure message
(with the resume-from-cache note) and exit 1.

Also: pin @types/node ^26 in cli and core - the desktop package's
electron deps introduced a second copy (24.x) and the CLI, which
never declared its own, began resolving conflicting instances
(ChildProcess.on vanished). Each package now states the version it
compiles against. CLI_REFERENCE ask section documents the floor.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git push -q origin main "+refs/notes/git-for-ai/*:refs/notes/git-for-ai/*" "+refs/git-for-ai/*:refs/git-for-ai/*" && git log --oneline -1
